knownFor.label: Fabergé eggs
knownFor.note: Jewelled Easter eggs made for the tsars.

knownFor.label: Trans-Siberian Railway
knownFor.note: The world’s longest railway line, completed in 1916.

knownFor.label: Cossacks
knownFor.note: Frontier horsemen who served as cavalry.

knownFor.label: Russian novels
knownFor.note: Tolstoy’s War and Peace (1869) and Dostoevsky’s works.

location.value: Most of northern Eurasia, from Poland and Finland to the Pacific, including Siberia, the Caucasus and Central Asia. It also held Alaska until 1867.

terrain.value: Vast plains, forest (taiga), tundra and steppe, with great rivers (Volga, Dnieper, Ob, Yenisei). Access to warm-water ports was limited.

climate.value: Cold continental climate with a short growing season. The harsh winter of 1812 contributed to the destruction of Napoleon’s army.

resources.value: Grain (a major export), furs, timber, and later coal, iron and oil (Baku).

disasters.value: The famine of 1891–92 and cholera epidemics in the 19th century.

population.value: About 16 million (1720), 38 million (1795), 74 million (1858), 126 million (1897 census) and 164 million (1914), including newly acquired territories.

urbanisation.value: Mostly rural. Saint Petersburg (founded 1703) and Moscow were the great cities, and industrial towns grew after the 1890s.

disease.value: Cholera and typhus epidemics struck repeatedly in the 19th century.

migration.value: Settlement of Siberia, the steppe and Central Asia, and large emigration of Jews and others to the Americas from the 1880s.

economicBase.value: An overwhelmingly agricultural economy built on serf labour, with rapid industrialisation (railways, mining) from the 1890s.

tradeRoutes.value: Baltic and Black Sea ports for grain exports. The Trans-Siberian Railway (1891–1916) linked Europe and the Pacific.

wealth.value: Less industrialised, with lower average incomes than Western Europe in the 18th century, according to Wikipedia. Industrial output grew fast after 1890 but remained low per person.

moneyAndTax.value: The ruble. Revenue rose from 9 million rubles in 1724 to 40 million in 1794, with spending at 49 million in 1794. Paper money and foreign loans caused inflation.

inequality.value: Extreme: a landed nobility over tens of millions of serfs until the emancipation of 1861 (about 23 million serfs freed).

governmentType.value: An absolute monarchy under the emperor (tsar), 1721–1906, then a semi-constitutional monarchy with the State Duma (1906–1917), though ultimate authority stayed with the tsar.

keyRulers.value: Peter I the Great (emperor 1721–1725). Catherine II the Great (1762–1796). Alexander I (1801–1825). Alexander II (1855–1881, the emancipation of the serfs). Nicholas II (1894–1917, last).

succession.value: Hereditary in the Romanov dynasty, but palace coups were common in the 18th century (e.g. Catherine II overthrew Peter III in 1762).

institutions.value: The Senate and Holy Synod (replacing the patriarchate), the Table of Ranks (1722), the 1861 emancipation, zemstvo local councils (1864), the October Manifesto (1905) and the State Duma.

stability.value: Pugachev’s Cossack and peasant uprising (1773), the Decembrist revolt (1825), Polish uprisings (1830, 1863), the assassination of Alexander II (1881), the 1905 Revolution, and the 1917 revolutions.

eliteConflict.value: Tension between reformers and conservatives at court, and between the autocracy and liberal and revolutionary movements.

armyAndTech.value: One of Europe’s largest armies, built by Peter I with a Baltic navy, but technologically behind its rivals by the Crimean War.

majorWars.value: The Great Northern War (to 1721). Wars with the Ottomans and Persia. Napoleon’s invasion (1812). The Crimean War (1853–56). The Russo-Japanese War (1904–05). The First World War (from 1914).

territoryChange.value: From about 15 million km² (1725) to a peak of 22.8 million km² (1895), about one-sixth of the world’s land and the third-largest empire in history.

alliancesRivals.value: Rivals: Sweden, the Ottomans, Persia, Napoleonic France, Britain (“the Great Game”), Japan and Germany. Allies: Austria and Prussia (the Holy Alliance), and France and Britain (from 1894/1907).

inventions.value: Peter I imported Western technology and shipbuilding. Later scientists included Lomonosov and Mendeleev (periodic table, 1869).

scienceEducation.value: The Academy of Sciences, Moscow University (1755), and the first newspaper (Vedomosti). Most of the population remained illiterate in the 18th century.

openness.value: Westernisation under Peter I and Catherine II, then periods of reaction (e.g. Nicholas I’s “Orthodoxy, Autocracy and Nationality”).

communicationTransport.value: Rivers, the post-horse system, railways from 1837 and the Trans-Siberian Railway (1891–1916); the telegraph.

religion.value: Eastern Orthodoxy was official (69.3% in 1897), with Catholics (9.2%), Muslims (11.1%), Jews (4.2%) and others.

languageWriting.value: Russian (official), with Finnish, German, Polish, Swedish and many other languages in a multi-ethnic empire.

artsArchitecture.value: Saint Petersburg’s baroque and neoclassical palaces, and a golden age of literature and music: Pushkin, Tolstoy, Dostoevsky, Tchaikovsky.

socialStructure.value: Tsar, nobility, clergy, merchants, Cossacks and a huge serf peasantry (serfs were tied to the land until 1861).

sharedIdentity.value: Loyalty to tsar and Orthodox Church. Russification policies (late 19th century) tried to impose Russian identity on minorities.

dailyLife.value: Peasants in wooden izbas; nobles in town houses; rye bread, kasha, cabbage soup and tea from the samovar.

neighbours.value: Sweden, Poland–Lithuania (partitioned), Prussia/Germany, Austria, the Ottoman Empire, Persia, the Central Asian khanates, Qing China and Japan.

ideasReligions.value: Imported Enlightenment, liberal and socialist ideas from Europe. Spread Orthodoxy and Russian culture to new territories.

colonisation.value: A land-based colonial empire: expanded across Siberia, the Caucasus and Central Asia, often by conquest, and colonised Alaska (1799–1867).

riseSignals.value: Ivan III’s centralised state, Ivan IV’s conquests, rapid eastward growth (about 35,000 km² a year from 1550 to 1700), and Peter I’s modernisation and victory over Sweden.

peakPeriod.value: Territorial peak in the late 19th century (22.8 million km² in 1895). Political prestige after defeating Napoleon (1812–15).

declineSignals.value: Defeat in the Crimean War, slow reform, defeat by Japan (1905), revolutionary movements, and the massive losses and shortages of the First World War.

outcome.value: Revolution. The February Revolution (1917) forced Nicholas II to abdicate, and a republic was proclaimed. The Bolsheviks took power in October 1917, and the Soviet Union was formed in 1922.

sources.value: State records, the 1897 census, memoirs and literature. Checked against Wikipedia on 5 Nov 2026. See also Hosking (1997).

overallCertainty.value: Good, with census data from 1897. Early population figures differ (14 or 16 million around 1720), and dates use both Old and New Style calendars.
